quote: We were gonna go with, you know, Aurora solar or something like that. But, apparently, they just filed bankruptcy. Freedom Pro. Sorry. Freedom Pro.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior competitor relationship and its collapse — real competitive intel — but the rep only reacts with sympathy and moves on rather than asking what was shown or promised.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that probing competitor specifics wasn't worth the call time given the customer was already cooperative and short on time before Saturday.
coaching_implication: A single follow-up ('what had they quoted you?') costs seconds and gives the closer useful comparison context; note Ion's competitive_landscape catalog is itself schema-TBD, so this is a missed low-cost opportunity rather than a quantifiable lost-value event.

quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be under my my mom and dad's name. I live here with them, so the the entire program will be under their name.
stewart_read: This is the adult-child-decision-maker pattern — customer lives with and is acting on behalf of the actual titleholders (parents) — but the rep never secures their presence on the Saturday appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be tracking this as resolved because the customer later insists it's his decision alone at 05:33, making a spouse-style intervention seem unnecessary in the moment.
coaching_implication: Per protocol, the co-decision-maker (here, the parents as titleholders) should be invited onto the appointment explicitly — 'let's make sure your parents can join since it's under their name' — rather than letting the customer's self-assertion of authority go unchallenged.

quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be me making a decision. I mean, technically, it is my house. So that's why I'm the one that's the decision maker.
stewart_read: This directly contradicts the 02:03 statement that the home and program will be under his parents' name — the rep doesn't reconcile the two statements or clarify who legally needs to be present for the sale to proceed.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep simply accepted the more convenient answer to keep momentum toward booking. Strategic read is weak here since no explicit reasoning or deferred plan is voiced by the rep.
coaching_implication: Flag this contradiction directly with the rep — the appointment is booked on an unresolved ownership question, which is a paycheck risk if the closer discovers at proposal that the customer isn't actually the titleholder or decision authority.

quote: My last was 1348. Okay. And do you see what you have? I have a Tesla phone. I have a Tesla, so it's gonna be a little bit more.
stewart_read: Customer hands over a usage figure and volunteers he has a Tesla (likely an EV, which increases electric load) — an enthusiasm signal for higher future usage — but the rep only acknowledges with 'Okay. Okay.' and moves to a different qualifying question instead of anchoring on it.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the figure ambiguous (kWh vs. dollars was never clarified) and chose not to build on an unverified number rather than risk anchoring on the wrong metric.
coaching_implication: Two things to flag: first, the number's unit was never confirmed as kWh; second, even taking it as usage, the rep could have reflected the Tesla-driven usage increase back ('so your usage is going to keep climbing with the EV — good timing to look into this now') instead of filing it silently.

quote: I have a Tesla, so it's gonna be a little bit more.
stewart_read: An EV in the household is a classic enthusiasm signal — higher electric load justifying solar — but it passes without the rep reflecting it back to the customer as a reason to move forward.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to catch and voice these signals live; even a single line tying the EV to future bill growth reinforces the customer's own stated motivation and strengthens the appointment's footing.

quote: Well, I have you in our calendar for this Saturday. That's the eight Can you can you ping me as soon as you're on the way so that I know your ETA, and then I I can make sure I'm on home accordingly?
stewart_read: The appointment gets a day and a window (2-5 on Saturday) but no locked specific time within that window, and the rep never runs the 'is that fair' handshake or the no-driving/computer instructions before hanging up.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep did state 2:00 at 06:35 ('I can have someone meet with you this Saturday at 02:00'), so a specific time was in fact offered — the miss is narrower: no explicit handshake confirmation and no computer/no-driving framing, given this appears to be an in-person visit rather than the phone-appointment structure the schema's button_up section assumes.
coaching_implication: Confirm with the rep whether this market runs in-person closer visits (the customer talks about someone driving to the house) — if so, the no-driving/computer script line doesn't directly apply, but the verbal handshake and a locked exact time still should be nailed down before ending the call.

quote: since we're doing locally, we have specialists in the area who would meet with you and bring that evaluation over. And because you're not in Tesla, so if you want to get a system size just a little bigger than what you're producing, we we tailor a system to fit your needs.
stewart_read: Rep begins explaining system-sizing logic and local/state incentive mechanics — closer-tier content — rather than using the universal escape hatch and redirecting straight to scheduling.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as necessary context-setting to justify why an in-person visit (rather than a phone call) is required, which is a legitimate scheduling-logistics explanation rather than true scope creep.
coaching_implication: Trim this explanation down; the rep can justify the in-person visit without wading into system-sizing specifics — save that for the specialist to build curiosity rather than pre-explain.
